_work.title: Kitāb Shumūs al-anwār wa-kunūz al-asrār (Princeton, Garrett 3182Y, 19c Arabic)
_work.blurb: A 19th-century Arabic composite codex held at Princeton University Library (Islamic Manuscripts, Garrett no. 3182Y), covering the full range of Islamic occult sciences in thirty-plus chapters. Its title — Shumūs al-anwār wa-kunūz al-asrār (Suns of Lights and Treasuries of Secrets) — signals its ambition: a comprehensive practitioner's treasury drawing on ʻilm al-ḥurūf (letter science), wafq (magic squares), practical talismanic operations, military magic, mineral alchemy, and geomantic divination for locating buried treasure. Unlike systematic theoretical treatises, this compendium presents knowledge as a step-by-step operational guide: each chapter names a divine attribute or magical goal and provides the associated wafq or sigil form, incense, ritual timing, and instructions. Diagrams appear in three distinct forms: (1) inline sigil illustrations using the 'shape like this' (صورة هكذا) convention, showing small drawn talisman forms directly in the running text; (2) embedded magic square grids (wafq) of 4×4 or larger format associated with specific divine names; (3) large operational jadwal (correspondence tables) correlating celestial or elemental categories with specific ritual actions; and (4) geometric divinatory diagrams for locating buried treasure (dafīna), showing a diamond-within-square sacred geometry template. Authorship is uncertain — the text has been attributed to Ibn al-Ḥājj (d. 1336) but may be later. Princeton University Library, Islamicmss collection, figgy UUID 567baddd.
_work.rights: Public Domain — 19th century CE manuscript. Princeton University Library.
_work.creator: attributed to Ibn al-Ḥājj Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad (d. 1336); anonymous copyist (19th century)

entries.title: Inline Talisman Sigil Drawings — Wafq for Water, Pearl, and Other Elements (f. 2r)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, inline drawn figures
entries.summary: A page from the Princeton Shumūs al-anwār wa-kunūz al-asrār (Garrett 3182Y, 19c) demonstrating the 'shape like this' (صورة هكذا) convention for inline talisman illustration, in which the author interrupts the running Arabic text to draw the actual geometric or letter-based sigil form directly on the page. The folio contains multiple such inline sigil drawings embedded mid-sentence: 'وفق للمياه صورة هكذا' (wafq for water, shape like this) followed by a drawn square or cross-grid sigil; 'وفق اللؤلؤ صورة هكذا' (wafq for pearl/treasure) followed by another compact drawn form; 'وفق الزياي صورة هكذا' followed by a geometric symbol. Each sigil is drawn freehand within the line spacing of the Arabic text rather than as a separate illustrated diagram, creating an unusual visual register where drawn magical forms interrupt and inhabit the flowing script. This 'صورة هكذا' (shape-like-this) convention is a distinctive feature of practical Islamic occult manuscripts — unlike systematic treatises that present diagrams on dedicated pages, this compendium integrates the visual form directly into the instructional text so the practitioner can see exactly what form to draw or inscribe on a talisman while reading the accompanying ritual instructions. The sigils shown relate to elemental and material correspondences (water, pearl) used in talisman construction.

entries.title: 4×4 Numeric Magic Square (Wafq) — Divine Name al-Ḥafīẓ (f. 8r)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, bordered grid
entries.summary: A page from the Princeton Shumūs al-anwār wa-kunūz al-asrār (Garrett 3182Y, 19c) containing a 4×4 numeric magic square (wafq) embedded mid-chapter, associated with the divine name al-Ḥafīẓ (الحفيظ, The Preserver/Guardian, one of the 99 names of God). The bordered square grid contains 16 cells arranged in a 4-row × 4-column format, filled with Arabic numerals and letter-numbers using the abjad system. Specific cell values are highlighted in red ink. The surrounding text (in dense Arabic naskh) discusses the spiritual properties and operational uses of this divine name — protective functions, guarding against enemies, preserving from harm — and gives instructions for when and how to write the wafq (specific days, times, materials, fumigations). The 4×4 magic square associated with specific divine names is a core format in the Islamic huruf tradition: each of the 99 divine names corresponds to a set of numerical values (via abjad letter-counting), and these values are used to construct a magic square where each row, column, and diagonal sums to the same total — making the wafq a visualization of the divine name's numerical essence. The embedded format (wafq appearing within a text page rather than on a dedicated diagram page) is characteristic of this compendium's practical orientation.

entries.title: Large Letter-Word Wafq Table — Quranic Name Operations Grid (f. 14r)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, red-bordered grid
entries.summary: A page from the Princeton Shumūs al-anwār wa-kunūz al-asrār (Garrett 3182Y, 19c) containing a large jadwal (correspondence table) occupying the lower half of the folio, following introductory text that ends with the phrase 'قوله تعالى' (the word of God Most High), indicating the table encodes Quranic names or phrases. The bordered rectangular grid is approximately 10 columns × 8 rows, with each cell containing a short Arabic word or phrase-fragment — the entries are letter combinations or abbreviated divine names rather than single letters or pure numerals. Row labels appear in the left margin identifying the operational categories, while column headers across the top designate day, time, or celestial correspondences. Some cells are written in red ink, marking particularly powerful or specific entries. Unlike the small 4×4 wafq squares, this large multi-column table is a jadwal format — a reference table mapping a two-dimensional matrix of magical parameters (divine names × timing) to specific outcomes or required inscriptions. The table is used as a lookup tool: the practitioner identifies the desired operation and the current day/hour, finds the corresponding cell, and uses its content as the basis for talisman inscription. This operational format represents the fully systematized form of Islamic huruf (letter science) practice.

entries.title: Military Operations Jadwal — Routing Enemy Armies Table (f. 20r)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, bordered grid
entries.summary: A page from Chapter Six ('On Routing Armies', الباب السادس في تهزيم الجيوش) of the Princeton Shumūs al-anwār wa-kunūz al-asrār (Garrett 3182Y, 19c), containing a large military operations jadwal (correspondence table) covering the lower half of the folio. The introductory text instructs the practitioner that this chapter concerns 'routing the disbelievers and the unjust' using Islamic magical means, and refers the reader to the table for complete operational guidance. The bordered grid is approximately 8 rows × 9-10 columns. The column headers across the top include zodiac signs (سنبلة / Virgo visible) and other astrological/celestial designations that determine which operation to use based on current celestial conditions. The row labels on the left identify different tactical components or elements of the military operation (types of forces, materials, procedures). Each cell contains the specific formula, incense, or action appropriate to that intersection of tactical goal and celestial timing. This is an unusually explicit table format for military or offensive magic — most Islamic occult compilations frame battlefield operations metaphorically or in general protective terms, but this chapter presents a systematic reference grid for a practitioner undertaking military campaigns. The use of astrological timing (zodiac columns) reflects the fusion of Islamic stellar magic (tanjīm) with the huruf tradition.

entries.title: Diamond-Within-Square Divinatory Diagram — Locating Buried Treasure (f. 38r)
entries.medium: manuscript, ink on paper, geometric diagram with text labels
entries.summary: A striking geometric diagram from the Princeton Shumūs al-anwār wa-kunūz al-asrār (Garrett 3182Y, 19c), appearing within a chapter on 'Istikhara' (استخارة — divine guidance divination) and specifically for 'tarbīʻ ʻalā mawḍaʻ al-dafīna' (squaring over the location of buried treasure). The diagram shows a large rotated square (diamond form) inscribed within or bordered by a square frame, with the diamond's four points directed toward the cardinal directions. The interior of the diamond is divided into triangular or trapezoidal sections by the diagonals, with text labels in each section identifying directional, elemental, or spiritual values (names like 'Abū Bakr', directional designations, or angelic names at each point). At the center of the diamond is a small grid of 3×3 or 4×4 cells containing letters or numbers. Text to the right of the diagram continues the operational instructions, mentioning specific conditions under which the practitioner applies this template over a suspected treasure site. The diamond-within-square format is related to the Islamic geomantic (raml) tradition and the divinatory practice of applying a geometric template to physical space — the diagram is both a mystical geometric form and a practical survey tool for spiritual treasure-hunting. The use of istikhara (a prayer-based divination seeking divine guidance) combined with a geometric talisman reflects the fusion of Islamic religious practice with occult geometry characteristic of this genre of manuscript.
